title: Budget e-bike conversion kit
summary: Custom motor control, a printed hub motor, and a simple goal: make electric transportation more accessible.

sections.title: The starting point
sections.text: I wanted to make electric transportation more affordable by converting a bicycle someone already owns. I set a materials-cost target below $150, with a stretch goal below $100, and split the kit into rider controls, a removable battery and electronics enclosure, and a motor.

sections.title: Designing across disciplines
sections.text: I designed the control board, battery housing, mounting system, and experimental brushless motor. The electronics brought together a custom brushless speed controller, an Arduino-based prototype, Bluetooth communication, and a thumb throttle. PETG housings and TPU seals were part of the enclosure design; these were prototype design choices, not a certified ingress-protection rating.

sections.title: Fifty boards, and a better process
sections.text: I initially manufactured the PCBs on my homemade CNC mill. Without solder mask, dense boards were difficult to assemble reliably. After more than 50 attempts, I stepped back and changed the process: outsourcing board fabrication and using integrated gate drivers. The lesson was to recognize when my tools had become the constraint.

sections.title: What the prototype demonstrated
sections.text: Bench tests demonstrated motor control with a small brushless motor, back-EMF sensing, throttle input, and Bluetooth data exchange with an iPhone. I also built and tested an iron-filled PLA motor with a Halbach magnet arrangement. The printed motor turned, but heat softened the plastic under load. That thermal limitation kept it from being a finished, road-ready kit.

sections.title: Where I would take it next
sections.text: The next step was to replace the printed stator with a conventional laminated metal core while keeping the custom electronics and enclosure. My 2024 component tally was $82.74 excluding the motor; that was a historical prototype estimate, not a retail price or a complete production bill of materials.

title: Desktop CNC / PCB mill
summary: Building the tool behind the projects: a compact, 3D-printed machine for milling custom circuit boards.

sections.title: A tool I could build myself
sections.text: I wanted a low-cost way to make circuit boards for my own projects. Building the mill became a project in its own right: mechanical design, fabrication, and learning what small-scale manufacturing could realistically do.

sections.title: The first version taught me about rigidity
sections.text: My first design used inexpensive plated rods and resin-printed linear bearings. Friction, poor stability, and limited rigidity made it unsuitable for accurate PCB work. Subsequent versions improved the machine enough to produce boards for my electronics projects.

sections.title: Useful capability, real limits
sections.text: The mill produced double-sided copper boards for the e-bike project. It also made the limits of my process clear: I could mill traces, but I could not add solder mask or reproduce all the features of professionally manufactured boards. Dense assemblies eventually justified outsourcing PCB fabrication.

sections.title: Why this one matters
sections.text: Making my own manufacturing equipment changed how I design parts. I had to understand the relationship between accuracy, stiffness, cost, and assembly, then carry those lessons into the projects the machine enabled.

title: Mini Cybertruck go-kart
summary: A homemade steel-frame go-kart with electronic steering, remote control, and a custom starter-generator.

sections.title: From wood to welded steel
sections.text: The project began with a wooden go-kart built over several summers. Repeated damage exposed the limits of that material and led to a steel-frame version. I sourced scrap steel, worked from CAD designs, and continued the build under a tent in my backyard during the winter.

sections.title: Making the controls electronic
sections.text: I built a steering actuator with a high-torque motor, a printed steering horn, and potentiometer feedback. The steering wheel itself used a spring return, with separate triggers for the throttle and brakes. Electronic control also made remote operation possible.

sections.title: One motor, two jobs
sections.text: The most interesting mechanism was a motor that could start the engine and then act as a generator. A printed belt transmission and one-way bearings changed the mechanical advantage from 9:1 during starting to 1:1 when the engine drove the motor. Withstanding the engine’s compression torque was a major manufacturing challenge.

sections.title: A whole system to integrate
sections.text: The build brought together steering, brake and throttle actuation, power distribution, an engine cutoff, lights, and servo-driven dashboard gauges. The 2024 documentation records a continuing integration effort, rather than a finished commercial vehicle.

title: Ion-thruster RC boat
summary: An experimental remote-controlled boat propelled by ionic wind, with no moving propulsion parts.

sections.title: An unusual way to move
sections.text: I explored whether an ionic-wind thruster could propel a small boat. The prototype used two independently driven thrusters, allowing differential steering without a conventional propeller or rudder.

sections.title: Geometry became the experiment
sections.text: Electrode geometry and spacing strongly influenced the result. My early tests compared different gaps, and adjustable mounts made it possible to iterate. The project notes also record a mismatch between advertised supply ratings and observed behavior, reinforcing the need to test assumptions.

sections.title: A demonstration, not a practical drivetrain
sections.text: The prototype produced a functioning, low-efficiency RC boat. Its value was as an experiment in electrostatic propulsion and hands-on testing, rather than as a competitive replacement for a motor-driven boat.

title: 3D-printed mechanical clock
summary: A gravity-driven clock and a hands-on lesson in friction, gear geometry, and tolerances.

sections.title: Keeping time mechanically
sections.text: I designed and printed a fully mechanical, gravity-driven clock. The project required a gear train and escapement that could run with very little available energy.

sections.title: Small friction, large consequences
sections.text: The high gear ratio meant that even slight friction near the escapement had a large effect on the drive requirements. I printed and tested many geometry and tolerance variations to improve the mechanism.

sections.title: A measurable improvement
sections.text: The documented iterations reduced the required counterweight mass by 75%. The discarded prototypes were essential to understanding how printed parts behave as a working mechanism.

imageAlt: 3D-printed mechanical clock — conceptual line illustration

title: Remote-controlled Hot Wheels
summary: A miniature RC car designed from scratch, complete with tank steering and its own charging case.

sections.title: A small car, a big learning curve
sections.text: My teacher proposed making a Hot Wheels-sized remote-controlled car. We took different approaches to steering: I chose differential drive and designed my own miniature body and chassis.

sections.title: Working at miniature scale
sections.text: I combined resin-printed wheels, TPU tires, and small motors and controller boards recovered from servos. Gear meshing and assembly tolerances were particularly challenging at this size.

sections.title: The finished object
sections.text: The final miniature Dodge Hellcat included underbody lighting and a portable AA-powered charging case. This was one of the first complex projects I pushed through to a working result, and its build video became a reminder to keep going on harder projects.

title: Automated hydroponic grow farm
summary: From lettuce in repurposed containers to shelves of automatically watered microgreens.

sections.title: Starting with a question
sections.text: An early interest in hydroponics led me to build growing systems at home. I started with lettuce under LED lights in repurposed containers, then gradually expanded the scale and automation.

sections.title: Scaling to microgreens
sections.text: The later system used pine shelving and trays of microgreens. An Arduino controlled watering, the grow lights ran on a 16-hour cycle, and newly planted trays began in a dark incubation box.

sections.title: Learning through a living system
sections.text: Unlike a mechanism that can be switched off between tests, the plants needed consistent care. The project connected physical construction, basic electronics, and the practical challenge of keeping a system running.

title: Low-cost RC plane
summary: An original RC aircraft design refined through years of builds, flight attempts, repairs, and redesigns.

sections.title: Learning by launching
sections.text: I developed successive versions of my own remote-controlled plane over several years. Many early versions crashed, sending me back to the workbench to repair the aircraft and change the design.

sections.title: Iteration was the process
sections.text: Each failed flight helped expose a weakness and suggest the next change. By June 2023, the project record included a successful flight with the tenth version.

sections.title: The useful part of failure
sections.text: This project made persistence tangible. It was not enough to improve a drawing: I had to build the revision, take it back outside, and try again.

title: Hybrid RC car
summary: A conversion project combining electric and nitro power, with an automatic starter.

sections.title: Combining two power sources
sections.text: I designed a conversion for a Traxxas nitro RC car to add electric power and an automatic starting system. The project is recorded as completed in May 2023.

sections.title: A connection to larger projects
sections.text: The interest in integrating combustion engines and electric machines also appears in my go-kart’s starter-generator system. Both projects explore the interfaces between motors, engines, and power transmission.

title: Industrial robotic vacuum
summary: A school-scale robotic vacuum with a custom 3D-printed cyclone assembly.

sections.title: A useful machine for school
sections.text: I designed and built a robotic vacuum for my school. The build combined the physical cleaning mechanism with a mobile platform.

sections.title: Making the airflow components
sections.text: The project included a printed cyclone vacuum assembly. Experimenting with its rotating components later informed the impeller work for my go-kart project.

sections.title: Documented in motion
sections.text: The project was recorded as completed in May 2022, with videos of the machine operating. The linked demonstrations show the build in use.

title: Universal arcade cabinet
summary: A Raspberry Pi arcade cabinet built with my brother from inexpensive wood and a repurposed monitor.

sections.title: A build with my brother
sections.text: We sourced inexpensive wood and built an arcade cabinet around a Raspberry Pi and a repurposed PC monitor. Unlike my other original projects, this cabinet used a design we found on YouTube.

sections.title: Making the interface
sections.text: We drilled the control panel for joysticks and buttons and connected them to an IPAC 4 board. The interface translated the controls into keyboard inputs for the Raspberry Pi.

sections.title: From materials to a playable machine
sections.text: The project brought together cabinet construction, wiring, and setup in a finished object we could actually use. It was completed by March 2022.

title: Gimbaling thrust-vector control
summary: A prototype exploration of a printed pitch-and-yaw gimbal and ground-test hardware.

sections.title: The mechanical question
sections.text: I explored a 3D-printed gimbal for pitch-and-yaw control as part of an early rocket project. The project brought together mechanism design and experimental ground testing.

sections.title: A test that exposed a material limit
sections.text: Early ground-test hardware failed to retain its geometry under heat. The result underlined the gap between a part that works in CAD and one that survives its operating environment. The record does not establish a successful guided flight.
